problem: Training-free LLM pruning methods (Magnitude, Wanda) with hardware-friendly 50% 2:4 structured sparsity lose little accuracy on LLMs. Applied to Vision-Language-Action models, they break them. OpenVLA drops from 85.2% to 0.0% success on LIBERO and NaVILA from 43.0% to 0.0% on VLN-CE-Isaac, and unsafe episodes rise (NaVILA with Magnitude pruning reaches 100% unsafe). No prior work studied pruning VLAs or how to recover the lost capability.
motivation: Robots deploy on memory- and power-limited hardware (e.g. Jetson Orin NX with 8–16 GB shared memory), while 7–8B VLAs need about 16 GB, so compression is necessary. A spectral comparison of matched layers in LLaMA-2-7B and OpenVLA explains why VLAs are fragile. VLA weight spectra decay more flatly, so energy is spread over many directions, and pruning small coefficients removes useful signal instead of only trimming low-energy directions.
key_idea: Keep the 2:4-pruned weights unchanged and add, per linear layer, a rank-r correction A(Bᵀx) taken from the truncated SVD of the gap between the dense and pruned weights. This re-injects the dominant lost directions without any training.
insight: Pruning discards signal concentrated in a few dominant directions of the weight gap. Re-adding only those top singular directions recovers most of the behaviour, because the sparse matrix still holds structure that low-rank alone cannot capture. Three ablations support this. (1) A rank-200 SVD of OpenVLA's weights without pruning gets 0% on LIBERO-Spatial, so pruned weights plus a low-rank gap beats low-rank alone. (2) Choosing singular components at random instead of by magnitude recovers only about 10% of the success that top-r selection achieves. (3) Rank r is a clean dial: on NaVILA, GLUESTICK-200 saves 5.36 GB with a −2.0 SR change and GLUESTICK-500 saves 4.60 GB with +1.0. Component sensitivity also matters: per parameter, pruning the vision backbone is 4.75× (OpenVLA) and 37.5× (NaVILA) more damaging than pruning the language backbone, so the authors prune mainly the language backbone.
method: Baseline pruning: Wanda (activation-aware magnitude scoring) enforces strict 50% 2:4 structured sparsity on linear layers. Calibration uses 15K LIBERO states for the manipulation models and 1K samples for NaVILA; the main setting prunes the language backbone and keeps the vision encoder dense.
Gap matrix: for each linear layer, W_gap = W_dense − W_pruned captures the information removed by pruning.

Truncated SVD correction (offline, one-time): W_gap ≈ U_r Σ_r V_rᵀ, the best rank-r Frobenius approximation (Eckart–Young). Singular values are folded into A = U_r Σ_r (d_out×r), and B = V_r (d_in×r) is stored alongside.
Online wrapper: h(x) = W_pruned x + A(Bᵀx). The sparse matmul keeps its 2:4 kernel benefits and the correction adds O((d_in+d_out)r) compute and (d_in+d_out)r parameters per layer.
Single hyperparameter r (GLUESTICK-r, r ∈ {10, 25, 100, 200, 500} in the ablation) trades memory against recovery; it is pruning-algorithm-agnostic.

Targeted calibration set, adopted as part of GLUESTICK: 3.5K states in a 5% window around the first gripper-closing event. This improves Wanda's pruned-language-backbone OpenVLA on LIBERO-Spatial from 31.2% to 33.4%.

setting.backbone: NaVILA-8B for navigation; OpenVLA-7B and WorldVLA-7B for manipulation. All are pretrained and frozen, then pruned with Wanda 2:4 and corrected with GLUESTICK; no weight training.
setting.model_size: 7B (OpenVLA, WorldVLA), 8B (NaVILA; 8.5B total parameters per the paper)
setting.training_data: none (training-free). Uses the officially released checkpoints (OpenVLA/WorldVLA LIBERO-suite fine-tunes, NaVILA). Wanda calibration data: 15K states from the LIBERO fine-tuning corpus (or a 3.5K gripper-event window) and a 1K calibration set for NaVILA.
setting.observation: NaVILA: egocentric monocular RGB (current frame plus history frames) and a language instruction. OpenVLA: RGB plus instruction. WorldVLA: current RGB plus one history image plus instruction.
setting.action_space: Navigation: velocity/mid-level commands (e.g. move forward 0.75 m, turn 15°) executed by a legged-robot locomotion controller. Manipulation: 7D end-effector pose plus gripper open/close (WorldVLA action chunk set to 1).
setting.simulator: Isaac Sim (VLN-CE-Isaac, Unitree Go2 / H1 legged robots); LIBERO for manipulation
setting.privileged: none (the method needs the dense weights offline to compute corrections; manipulation containment regions for the safety metric come from the ground-truth dataset, used for evaluation only)

numbers_note: Navigation results come only from NaVILA on a 100-episode random subset of VLN-CE-Isaac. Success and unsafe rates are printed as deltas vs dense (dense: 43.0% SR, 23.0% unsafe), so absolute GLUESTICK SR is not printed. Path Length (PL) is mapped to TL and final Distance to Goal (DG) to NE. The rank ablation (GLUESTICK-10/25/100/200/500 on LIBERO-Spatial: 0.6%, 7.4%, 18.6%, 30.8%, 57.4%) and the component-sensitivity ablation appear only in Figure 4. The rank-500 bar (57.4%) differs from Table 5's 60.2, possibly because of a different calibration set. There is a text/table inconsistency in Q3: the text says the memory-matched baseline raises unsafe episodes by '+7.5% and +8.4%' (these are LIBERO Table 4 values), while Table 3 shows +12.0 for the memory-matched baseline on navigation. The memory-matched baseline prunes 75% of layers (OpenVLA/WorldVLA) or 81.3% of layers (NaVILA). No latency or energy measurements are reported, only peak RAM.
results: On VLN-CE-Isaac, dense NaVILA scores 43.0% success and Wanda Full Sparse 0%. GLUESTICK-500 slightly exceeds dense on the success delta (+1.0), cuts unsafe episodes (−4.0), and restores path length and goal distance (11.9 m / 5.9 m vs dense 11.7 / 5.9) while saving 4.60 GB. The memory-matched sparse-backbone baseline instead loses −18.0 SR. On LIBERO, averaged over OpenVLA and WorldVLA, GLUESTICK-500 loses −35.7 SR vs −72.4 for Full Sparse and −59.3 for the memory-matched baseline, and keeps the unsafe-rate increase at +1.5 vs +13.6 for Full Sparse. OpenVLA LIBERO-Spatial recovers from 0.0% (Full Sparse) or 31.2% (sparse language backbone) to 60.2%.
limitations: The memory benefit largely disappears at the rank needed for good recovery: GLUESTICK-500 uses about the same RAM as the memory-matched baseline (11.97 vs 11.96 GB on OpenVLA). Real speed and energy gains from 2:4 sparse kernels plus the dense low-rank branch are not measured.

Manipulation recovery is partial: about 50% of the lost success on average, and WorldVLA on LIBERO-Long stays at 0%. Navigation is evaluated on only 100 episodes with one model (NaVILA), all in simulation, without real-robot tests.

The headline '% of lost performance recovered' is partly measured against Full Sparse, which also prunes the vision encoder, while GLUESTICK is applied to a language-backbone-only pruned model. Only Wanda at 50% 2:4 sparsity is evaluated as the base pruner despite the pruning-agnostic claim.
compares_to: Full Sparse (Wanda 2:4 on all linear layers)
